analysis.one_liner: Requires employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The Healthy Families Act was referred to the Senate committee it needed to clear in March 2013 and never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or any other action before Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employers with 15 or more employees to let workers earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours (seven workdays) a year. Workers could use the time for their own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, or partner, or to handle medical, legal, and safety needs after domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Employers with existing equally generous policies would not have to change anything. The bill was introduced by Senator Tom Harkin in March 2013, sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 percent of private-sector workers who lacked paid sick time when the bill was introduced, with the biggest gains going to low-wage workers: 71 percent of the lowest-earning quartile of private-sector workers had none. Workers also would have gained the right to use sick time to care for family members and to take time off to deal with domestic violence or stalking, and would be protected from being fired or disciplined for using it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers without paid sick days

how_it_helps.text: Employees at covered employers earn at least 1 hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for their own medical needs.

Sick time can also be used to care for a child, parent, spouse, domestic partner, or similar close relation, or to seek medical attention, relocate, or take legal action after domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

The bill cites findings that about 40 percent of the private-sector workforce and 25 percent of the public-sector workforce lacked paid sick time, rising to 71 percent of the lowest-earning quartile of private-sector workers.

It bars employers from firing, discriminating against, or retaliating against workers who use the leave, and gives the Labor Department and workers themselves enforcement tools, including civil suits for damages.

The bill's findings cite studies estimating universal paid sick days would cut preventable emergency-room visits, saving about $1.1 billion a year including roughly $500 million in Medicaid savings, and that a lack of such policies contributed to about 5 million extra flu-like illnesses during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers with 15 or more employees pay for the sick time itself and for recordkeeping, notice-posting, and compliance costs. Industries that run on low-wage hourly labor with thin margins — retail, food service, hospitality — would bear the largest share, and some employers might respond by cutting hours or hiring slower to offset the cost.

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a direct cost to employers: paid hours not worked, plus compliance, recordkeeping, and posted-notice requirements, which fall hardest on low-margin employers of hourly workers. The bill's own findings acknowledge the need to design the mandate to be 'feasible for employers.'

Employers could see scheduling friction when workers take unplanned leave, and while the bill lets employers require a doctor's note for absences longer than three consecutive workdays, it bars them from delaying the leave while waiting for that paperwork.

The 56-hour annual cap and the 15-employee threshold mean part-timers and employees of the smallest businesses get little or nothing, and workers who leave a job are not paid out for unused sick time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers without any paid sick time, the benefit is substantial: income protection during illness and the ability to see a doctor or care for a sick child without risking a paycheck or a job. The cost side is real but limited — a capped seven days a year, no cash-out at separation, and an exemption for existing equally generous policies and for employers under 15 workers. The main honest objection is the compliance burden on small and thin-margin employers and the risk that some respond by trimming hours. On balance, this was a broad, moderate benefit to ordinary workers with costs concentrated on employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate HELP committee in March 2013, and that was the last thing that ever happened to it — no markup, no floor vote, nothing — until the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced S. 631, the Healthy Families Act, in the Senate on March 20, 2013, joined by 17 original cosponsors including Senators Mikulski, Murray, Warren, Durbin, and Schumer.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced.
The bill accumulated 23 cosponsors — 22 Democrats and 1 Independent — but no Republican cosponsored it.

The full action history shows no further action of any kind after the March 20, 2013 referral; the committee never took it up and the Senate never voted on it before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have been required to provide paid sick days avoided the mandate, since the bill died in committee without a vote. Workers without paid sick time gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who never faced the mandate

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 23 Senate cosponsors (22 Democrats, 1 Independent)
for.role: Senate cosponsors, including Mikulski, Murray, Casey, Franken, Whitehouse, Murphy, Warren, Levin, Durbin, Schumer, Brown, Merkley, Gillibrand, Blumenthal, Hirono, and others
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them was a Republican.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired during the 113th Congress by the bill's own sponsor, Sen. Harkin, and then Sen. Murray
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or advanced the bill after referral; the bill's last recorded action was its March 20, 2013 referral to the committee.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader and party leadership of the 113th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents and no Republican signed on; with no votes ever held, the only measurable support in the record split entirely along party lines.

industries.industry: Low-wage service employers (retail, food service, hospitality, care work)
industries.note: These employers employ the bulk of the workers who lack paid sick time, so the mandate's cost — up to seven paid days per employee per year plus compliance — would have fallen on them most heavily. Their savings on the mandate are the wage floor and job protection workers would have gained.

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more employees generally
industries.note: Covered employers would bear the cost of the leave, recordkeeping under Fair Labor Standards Act-style rules, posted notices, and potential civil suits for interference with the right. Employers with existing equally generous policies were exempted from doing anything more.

industries.industry: Public and private health insurers (including Medicaid)
industries.note: The bill's findings cite an estimate that universal paid sick days would save payers about $1.1 billion a year by reducing preventable emergency-room visits, including roughly $500 million in Medicaid savings, from earlier routine care.
